prompt: A manufacturer launching a supply-chain resilience initiative (after a recent single-supplier disruption) needs a KPI scorecard to track progress. Design 4-6 KPIs.
context: Triggering event: a single sole-source supplier for a critical component caused a 6-week production stoppage this year. Post-incident review found that 34% of the company's critical components (by spend) currently have only one qualified supplier. The initiative's stated goals are to reduce single-source dependency and improve early-warning visibility into supplier risk, within an 18-month timeframe, without materially increasing procurement cost (a board-stated constraint).

binaryCriteria.description: Includes tracking the percentage of critical spend/components with only one qualified supplier, explicitly referencing the given 34% baseline to be reduced over the program.
binaryCriteria.guidance: Fail if this specific metric and baseline are absent from the scorecard.

binaryCriteria.description: Includes a leading, early-warning supplier-risk-visibility metric, matching the initiative's explicitly stated second goal.
binaryCriteria.guidance: Fail if only single-source percentage is tracked with no supplier-risk-visibility measure.

binaryCriteria.description: Includes a cost-impact/guardrail metric tracking procurement cost variance, given the explicit board constraint against materially increasing procurement cost.
binaryCriteria.guidance: Fail if no cost-guardrail metric is proposed despite the explicit board constraint.

goldNotes: A strong scorecard centers on the specific, quantified starting point given — % of critical spend with only one qualified supplier (currently 34%) — as the primary KPI to track down over the 18-month program, rather than a vague "supplier diversification" narrative with no baseline number. It should include a leading, early-warning-visibility metric (e.g., number/percentage of critical suppliers with an active risk-monitoring flag or equivalent), directly matching the initiative's stated second goal. Given the explicit board constraint of not materially increasing procurement cost, a strong scorecard should also include a cost-impact tracking metric (e.g., procurement cost variance attributable to the resilience program) as a guardrail KPI, not just a "good news" set of resilience metrics — omitting a cost guardrail given an explicit board constraint on cost would be a meaningful gap. A weak scorecard proposes generic supply-chain KPIs (e.g., on-time delivery) that are not tied to the specific single-source problem and stated goals in the context.
